text:
Source: Roblo x
Roblox lost nearly a third of its value after report ing it s Q2 2026 results at the end of July. The stock now trades near $37, about 75% below its 2025 peak and well below its listing price from five years ago. Around $70B in market value has evaporated over the past twelve months.
Roblox's business did not fall as heavily. In Q2, revenue grew 36% and daily active users (DAU) grew 10% YoY. Quarter over quarter, revenue is flat while DAU is declining.
Source: Naavik analysis
Roblox had an extraordinary 2025, and the market priced it for more of the same. So, it turns out, did management. That makes this an expectations reset more than a business failure. It is not only an expectations problem: Roblox was already cooling as it began making changes that added even more pressure on growth and monetization. The more interesting question is whether those changes are temporary self-inflicted pain or whether they are landing on top of a business that was slowing anyway.
Look at Bookings, Not Revenue
Roblox's reported revenue is a lagging indicator. When someone buys Robux, that money is recognized as revenue gradually over the estimated lifetime of a paying user (27 months at the company’s last disclosure). This makes the 36% YoY revenue growth an echo of last year's boom. Bookings, which capture the sale when the Robux is purchased, are the number that tells you what is happening right now.
Source: Roblox and Naavik analysis
Bookings grew 8% in Q2 year over year but declined quarter over quarter. The quarterly numbers are where the predicament shows up: DAU has declined for three consecutive quarters, bookings for two, and monthly unique payers have fallen alongside them. Spending per user fell too, with bookings per daily user down 2% YoY and bookings per payer down 6%. Fewer players, each spending a little less.
Three things stand out:
The decline predates the algorithm change. DAU peaked in Q3 2025 and bookings in Q4. April's discovery update landed on a platform that was already cooling.
Roblox is doing the worst where the money is. U.S. and Canada are the best-monetizing markets, and bookings there stayed essentially flat YoY. Meanwhile, Europe grew by 18%, Asia-Pacific by 14%, and the rest of the world by 31%.
The outlook is worse than the quarter. Roblox withdrew its full-year outlook and guided Q3 to a revenue growth of 4–10% and a bookings decline of 14–18%. It's the first bookings decline the company has ever guided to, and the main reason the stock crashed.
Some of the Pain is Self-Inflicted
A number of the biggest headwinds are the result of choices management made deliberately. That does not make them good choices: the case rests on whether today’s lost growth buys Roblox a stronger platform later.
The business is maturing. Nothing grows 20% a year forever. Roblox's stated ambition is 10% of global gaming content revenue. It currently has less than 4% of that market. That is both an enormous business and a long way from the target. The goal was always going to get harder as the base got bigger.
2025 was a spike, not a slope. Grow a Garden and the brainrot wave that followed it broke concurrent-player records and monetized far above anything Roblox could reasonably expect to repeat. Entertainment is hit-driven, and platforms are no exception. Developers keep getting better (and of course, there is even Grow a Garden 2 now), but you cannot commission lightning. Sustaining 70% growth was never realistic.
Safety adds friction. Age checks became mandatory for chat in January. It’s very much defensible, but it does put an extra step between a new user and the social interaction that Roblox is really about. Verification also shrank the adult audience on paper: the share of players Roblox counts as 18+ was lower once ages were verified rather than self-reported.
Discovery now optimizes for retention. Roblox expanded its Recommended For You algorithm from a 7-day view to a 28-day view, with separate signals for Day 1, Days 2–7, and Days 8–28. Roblox is deliberately sending fewer players toward the experiences that monetized hardest, and it says the effect on under-13 spending in North America was bigger than expected.
Both discovery and safety are better understood as investments than as headwinds.
Investing in safety is the clearest case. Right now, it is friction and legal expense. But in the long run, regulation is a tax on Roblox and a barrier to everyone smaller. It is also a precondition for the advertising business because you cannot sell targeted inventory against an audience whose ages you do not know.
Engagement-weighted discovery has precedent. YouTube famously shifted from clicks to watch time in 2012, and Google later applied similar thinking to Google Play. Early on, a UGC platform needs supply: more creators, more content, more reasons to open the app. Eventually, a successful platform drowns in content, and the real job becomes deciding what deserves an audience. This is what Roblox is now trying to solve, and what YouTube, Steam, the App Store, and Google Play all went through.
Roblox's platform is unusually vertically integrated. It owns discovery, payments, hosting, identity, and currency. Changing discovery redistributes income across an entire economy, which is why developers spent April watching their impressions move and arguing about whether it was a bug or the point. The question is subtler than "the algorithm hurt me." If distribution now depends on 28-day retention, how does a brand-new game ever prove it has any?
It also makes Roblox game studios harder to invest in or buy. Anyone writing a check wants to know what a game will earn next year, and that guess assumes traffic keeps behaving as it did last year. Roblox has to keep changing discovery, but predictability is worth something too.
A standalone publisher can survive a bad recommendation algorithm by getting traffic elsewhere. A Roblox developer has far fewer places to go. The healthier Roblox makes discovery for players, the more consequential (and potentially frustrating) its decisions become for creators.
The Long-Term Bet
Roblox’s bet is this: the company is deliberately accepting a worse 2026 in the hope that 2028 is better. The problem is that not all of 2026’s weakness was deliberate.
The good case is still compelling. Retention-focused discovery produces better games, safety changes make the platform easier to regulate and monetize, older users deepen the audience, and DAU growth resumes once the transition settles. Bookings recover.
The bad case is simpler. Roblox gets through the discovery transition and absorbs the safety friction, but growth still does not pick up; Roblox will have given up near-term bookings for nothing.
That is why the guidance misses matter. In February, Roblox told investors to expect 22–26% bookings growth in 2026. In April, it cut that to 8–12%. In July , it withdrew the outlook and guided Q3 to a decline. Naveen Chopra took over as CFO in mid-2025, so the February number was his first annual guide, and it lasted a single quarter.
Some of this is genuinely unforecastable, but not all of it. Roblox set that February number knowing its own age checks and its own algorithm change were coming, and misjudged both. Netflix spent years learning to guide a business it couldn't fully predict, and got good at it. Roblox has to do the same: test the changes before promising the results. Right now, management may be right about the destination, but it hasn’t shown it can price the trip.
Getting through the transition is only half the problem. Roblox still needs credible sources for future growth. Part of the answer is simple. Roblox needs more breakout hits. The 2025 surge came from content, and the next surge will too. What Roblox controls is whether the platform makes hits more likely: better tools, discovery that finds them early, and economics that keep the studios capable of building them.
The other part is aging up. Adults are 27% of age-checked daily users, and U.S. users over 18 monetize over 50% better than users under 18. Roblox now pays creators roughly 42% more on qualifying spend from age-checked American adults, a direct attempt to buy that content into existence. If bookings per user are going to rise without squeezing children harder, older players are the answer.
The question is whether Roblox understands what it needs to do to get them. Investor communications have leaned for two years on high-fidelity, AAA-grade experiences as the route to that audience, as though what keeps adults away were the graphics.
Roblox Build | Source: Roblox
The stronger argument is that older players want depth: persistent economies, progression that compounds, strategy, social competition, real cooperation. None of that needs AAA graphics, and most of it plays to what Roblox already is. The worst outcome is a console game trapped inside Roblox: more expensive than a Roblox game, worse than a real one.
Successful Roblox games already work like well-run mobile games: a steady drip of new content, rewards for logging in each day, seasonal challenges you pay to unlock, and carefully balanced in-game currencies. A discovery system that now rewards month-long retention only pushes developers further that way.
Roblox does not need to build those games itself. Nobody else in UGC gaming has a network this size, and nobody else can spend against it the way Roblox can. That advantage is real and it is not going away this year. With the newly introduced Build , Roblox is showing where a chunk of that spending goes: prompt-to-game creation inside the mobile app and agents in Studio for playtesting, analytics, and experiments. Developers have been lukewarm on in-engine AI assistants elsewhere, but Roblox might be better positioned than any other company to make it work. The bigger opportunity, though, is in the boring stuff done right: development and publishing tooling, analytics, moderation, discovery creators can plan around, and safety they inherit for free. This is what decides whether the next hit gets built here.
Investors now have to distinguish patience from excuses. The likeliest path is neither collapse nor a fast rebound; it’s a few more quarters of growing pains while the transition works through, and a company that comes out of it bigger than the one that went in.

Hello hello!
And welcome to another week on The Game Business.
You may have noticed we’ve changed the name of our Monday morning edition. It used to be called ‘The Game Business Micro’, and now we’ve gone with the sillier (but more accurate) ‘Here’s The Dring’.
When we started doing the Micro, it was just a news round-up. It was running through the stories of the previous seven days and providing you with the information you’d need for the week ahead.
We still do that, but it’s changed over time. Now, the bulk of the ‘Micro’ is original analysis, opinion and (sometimes) data. What’s more, although the podcast is still (relatively) short, the newsletter is actually quite chunky. So, I felt the name ‘Micro’ was both inaccurate and undersold what we were making. Hence the new name.
Out of the three newsletter/podcasts that we do, this is the one that sits behind our paywall. And we have a special Summer Sale on right now. For the next two weeks, you can get yourself an annual subscription to The Game Business at 25% off. Alongside ‘Here’s The Dring’ every Monday, you’ll also get our monthly market report and you can come to our Los Angeles event in June at no extra cost. Plus, you’ll help fund all the big free interviews we do. Want to support us? Click the button below to sign-up.
There are load of stories in this week’s edition, and the two I’ve focused on includes Netflix’s surprising decision to close its best studio, and 2K’s equally surprising decision to open a new sports developer in the same city as EA Sports.
Let’s dive in!
2K opens a sports developer on EA’s lawn… is it making a football game?
In Brief: 2K Games has launched Small Axe Studios. The new developer is led by EA Sports veterans and is based in the same city: Vancouver, Canada. The team is building the ‘next blockbuster sports franchise’ and wants to ‘redefine the future of sports video games’.
What You Need To Know:
The studio is made up of former EA Sports development leaders including VP and executive producer Aaron McHardy (EA Sports FC, Madden), head of design Gary Paterson (FIFA, NBA Live), head of operations Tom Pan (FIFA, UFC, SSX), head of engineering Mike Thompson (NHL, UFC), and technical art director John Cruz (FIFA, NBA, Skate).
Other key hires include head of HR Trisha MacWan (Glu Mobile), animation director Brend Breedveld (Relic Entertainment) and art director Karl Gryc (Blackbird Interactive).
2K is already a major player in sports games, and is responsible for the NBA 2K, WWE 2K and PGA 2K franchises. Its main sports studio is Visual Concepts, which dates back to 1998 and was originally owned by Sega.
Many of the people working for Small Axe worked on the EA Sports FC/FIFA series, giving rise to the expectation that this developer is creating a new football/soccer game.
The company’s name is due to the belief that ‘ with vision, drive, and focus, a small axe can take down a big tree ’.
The studio came out of 2K Sports Lab, which was set-up in 2023 to research and develop future sports games.
My Take:
When EA ditched the FIFA licence in 2023 and rebranded its game as ‘EA Sports FC’, the football governing body was defiant.
FIFA president Gianni Infantino declared that the group would be back, and that “ the only authentic, real game that has the FIFA name will be the best one available“.
“Not a chance,” I said at the time. FIFA might have some success on mobile around the World Cup, and the FIFA World Cup cloud game that Netflix commissioned was an interesting idea… but ‘the only authentic, real game’? No way.
